research_question: How do current systems combine a graph data model with embeddings for storing, linking, and retrieving knowledge with provenance, which architectures achieve this with the fewest moving parts, and which of their concepts have been hardened through several documented rounds of formulation, criticism, and reformulation?
intended_use: Choose the technology of the knowledge graph with provenance: a personal or team knowledge system over news, email, chat, and transcripts, with the Agent Factory as first tenant. The technology is open. Candidates include a graph database with a custom embedding layer, and PostgreSQL with Apache AGE and pgvector. The survey favours simplicity and elegance: few components, one consistency boundary, one query path, rebuildable derived data. It informs the store decision in the case document and a later falsification study; it changes no factory code.
audience: Agent Factory maintainers who know software engineering and the two earlier surveys, but not the literature on vector retrieval, graph retrieval, or embedding quality.
scope: Four areas. (1) Architectures that combine graphs and embeddings: retrieval-augmented generation over knowledge graphs (GraphRAG and its successors), hybrid graph and vector retrieval, knowledge graph embeddings versus text embeddings of nodes and spans, and how each architecture keeps the graph and the vectors consistent. (2) Stores that hold both: PostgreSQL with Apache AGE and pgvector, PostgreSQL with SQL/PGQ where available, graph databases with native vector indexes (such as Neo4j, Memgraph, FalkorDB), embedded options (such as DuckDB with its graph and vector extensions), and a separate vector store beside a graph store. For each: data model, query language, transaction and consistency boundary, how a graph traversal and a similarity search run in one query, maturity, release activity, and project health. (3) Embedding similarity for the system's tasks: paraphrase, claim matching, text reuse, near-duplicate detection, and same-idea detection. What similarity finds, what it misses (negation, entailment direction, domain shift), and how vectors are versioned and recomputed when the model changes. (4) Approximate nearest neighbour indexes and hybrid queries: the index lineage (from locality-sensitive hashing through inverted files and product quantization to graph-based indexes such as HNSW and DiskANN), filtered vector search combined with structured predicates, and the cost of keeping an index current under updates. For each area, record the concepts that went through several documented rounds of proposal, criticism, and replacement, with the sequence of formulations and the criticism that drove each change. For each store or architecture, record the facts a simplicity comparison needs: number of components, number of query languages, consistency boundaries, and what must be kept in sync.
exclusions: Implementing, installing, or benchmarking any tool or store
Vendor marketing material as evidence for a claim about capability, performance, or adoption; vendor documentation counts only for stated features and syntax
Graph data models and standards already covered by the knowledge-graph-state-of-the-art survey, except where an area needs them as context
Pricing and licensing assessment of products, except whether a component is open source
Legal limits on storage, such as copyright and data protection
freshness_requirements: Stores, extensions, and retrieval systems: current documentation and release state as of November 2026
Retrieval and embedding research from 2020 onward
Older sources are acceptable and expected for the history of a concept, such as nearest-neighbour indexes from the 1990s onward
source_requirements: Primary sources first: original papers, project documentation, release notes, and repositories
Peer-reviewed surveys and benchmarks for the overview of each area
Each history of a concept cites the source of each formulation and of each criticism
Secondary sources only where a primary source is unreachable, and then marked as secondary
Every source record states what the source shows and what it does not show, and puts the source's own words in double quotes in its Evidence section
cost_of_error: High. The store choice is expensive to change once it holds data, and a component that is abandoned or inconsistent under updates would damage every layer. The survey must mark weak evidence and project-health risks rather than hide them.
completion_criteria: Each of the four scope areas has findings backed by recorded sources
The report compares the candidate store architectures on the simplicity facts in the scope, each fact backed by a record
The report states what embedding similarity can and cannot establish for each of the system's tasks, and how a similarity result becomes a graph edge only after a check
The report names the concepts with a documented history of several formulation and criticism rounds, checked by concept-history-check
The report lists candidates for the later falsification study, phrased as testable design claims, including at least one claim per candidate store architecture
The report reports history as what the sources document; it does not claim that any concept survived refutation, because that verdict belongs to the falsification workflow
